mainTopic: רב אשי's fix for רבי יהודה's contradiction, the sources for reading on the fifteenth in walled cities, and the dispute over which walls count
overview: The amud opens by finishing רב אשי's fix. A ברייתא and a משנה seem to have רבי יהודה contradicting himself about villages reading the מגילה early, so רב אשי says the ברייתא belongs to רבי יוסי בר יהודה. The גמרא asks how he could change a name just because of a question. It answers that he had heard both versions and chose the precise one. Next, רבא finds a source for walled cities reading on the fifteenth. The גמרא then rules out the other options: no פורים at all, both days, a free choice, or the thirteenth. A הקש then ties the reading of the מגילה to the days of celebration. The גמרא compares our משנה, which counts walls from יהושע בן נון, with רבי יהושע בן קרחה, who counts them from אחשורוש. Along the way it explains why שושן is an exception and how each side reads 'מדינה ומדינה ועיר ועיר'. Finally, רבי יהושע בן לוי rules that places within a מיל of a walled city count as walled, and the amud begins a new topic about the final letters מנצפך, a challenge that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב אשי assigns the ברייתא to רבי יוסי בר יהודה
steps.stepSummary: This is the end of רב אשי's move. He says the ברייתא follows רבי יוסי בר יהודה, not רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he establishes the ברייתא as following רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: This amud opens in the middle of רב אשי's statement. He solves his problem by saying the ברייתא is really the opinion of רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי saw two statements in the name of רבי יהודה that disagree. His fix is to say the ברייתא was said by a different תנא, רבי יוסי בר יהודה. Once the ברייתא is not רבי יהודה's, the contradiction goes away. The next steps explain what the contradiction was.

keyTerms.meaning: He establishes it, meaning he explains whose opinion it is
A teaching of the תנאים that was not included in the משנה

phrases.english: and he establishes the baraita
phrases.notes: The 'he' here is רב אשי, from the previous amud.

phrases.english: in accordance with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמוֹקֵים לַהּ לְבָרַיְיתָא כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב אשי's statement from the end of earlier.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is רבי יהודה's opinion, so it contradicts the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is רבי יוסי בר יהודה's opinion, so there is no contradiction.

steps.title: The contradiction between the ברייתא and the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the problem. In the ברייתא, רבי יהודה says nowadays the מגילה is read only on its day. In the משנה, רבי יהודה lets places where villagers come to town on Monday and Thursday read early.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יהודה really say, 'Nowadays, since people look at the reading, we read it only on its proper day'? A משנה contradicts this. רבי יהודה said: When may villages read early? In a place where they come to town on Monday and Thursday. But in a place where they do not come on Monday and Thursday, they read it only on its proper day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what was bothering רב אשי. It quotes the ברייתא's version of רבי יהודה and sets it against a משנה in which רבי יהודה says something different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, רבי יהודה says that nowadays everyone reads on the 14th of אדר. That is because people use the reading of the מגילה to count 30 days until פסח. In the משנה (on 5a), רבי יהודה bans early reading only in places where villagers do not come to town on Monday and Thursday. That implies early reading is still allowed in places where they do come on Monday and Thursday.

keyTerms.meaning: People look at it, meaning they use the מגילה reading to count toward פסח
And they contradicted it. This introduces a source that clashes with the one just quoted.
On its proper time, the 14th of אדר
Monday and Thursday, the market and court days when villagers came to town

steps.confusionAlert: Both statements are said in the name of רבי יהודה. The problem is not a disagreement between two rabbis. It is one rabbi who seems to contradict himself.

phrases.english: But did Rabbi Yehuda really say:
"Nowadays, since people look to it (to calculate Passover),
we read it only in its proper time"?
And a contradiction was raised: Rabbi Yehuda said:
When (may they read early)? In a place where they enter town on Monday and Thursday.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין נִכְנָסִין בַּשֵּׁנִי וּבַחֲמִישִׁי —
phrases.english: But in a place where they do not enter on Monday and Thursday,
they read it only in its proper time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the difficulty that led to the fix in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement of רבי יהודה that nowadays the מגילה is read only on the 14th.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה quotes רבי יהודה as allowing early reading in some places. That clashes with a total ban nowadays.

steps.title: The inference: early reading is allowed even nowadays
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws out the point of the משנה. Where villagers come on Monday and Thursday, they read early, even nowadays.
steps.simpleTranslation: At least in a place where they come to town on Monday and Thursday, we read early, and that is even nowadays!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens the contradiction by stating exactly what the משנה implies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ties the rule to Monday and Thursday visits, not to the time period. So in towns with those visits, early reading is allowed even today. That directly opposes the ברייתא, which bans early reading nowadays.

phrases.english: A place where they enter on Monday and Thursday
at least, we do read (early),
and even nowadays!

steps.triggerLanguage: מְקוֹם שֶׁנִּכְנָסִין בַּשֵּׁנִי וּבַחֲמִישִׁי מִיהָא קָרֵינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contradiction by drawing the inference from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ban on early reading nowadays.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה allows early reading in Monday and Thursday towns, with no exception for nowadays.

steps.title: Restating רב אשי's fix
steps.stepSummary: Because of this contradiction, רב אשי said the ברייתא follows רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so he establishes the ברייתא as following רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the contradiction is clear, the גמרא repeats רב אשי's solution. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא will question that solution.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words repeat step 1, but now they serve a new purpose. They close the explanation of the contradiction and show why רב אשי changed the name. The גמרא repeats the solution so that it can challenge it.

phrases.english: And (therefore) he establishes the baraita
in accordance with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמוֹקֵים לַהּ לְבָרַיְיתָא כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ties the contradiction just explained back to רב אשי's solution.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both statements are רבי יהודה's, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא belongs to רבי יוסי בר יהודה.

steps.title: Surprise at changing the name to escape a contradiction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised. Would רב אשי really move a ברייתא to a different תנא just because he had a contradiction he could not answer?
steps.simpleTranslation: Just because he had a difficulty between רבי יהודה and רבי יהודה, he assigns the ברייתא to רבי יוסי בר יהודה?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges רב אשי's method. It questions whether you may change a name in a source just to get out of a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Changing who said a teaching is a drastic move. Normally the גמרא tries to explain away a contradiction rather than change the text. The challenge suggests רב אשי must have had a stronger reason. The next step gives that reason.

keyTerms.meaning: That it was difficult for him
רבי יהודה against רבי יהודה, meaning one rabbi contradicting himself

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a basic rule of how the גמרא works. A source is not changed just because it is hard to understand. A text change needs real support.

phrases.english: And because it was difficult for him
(the contradiction) of Rabbi Yehuda against Rabbi Yehuda,
he establishes the baraita
in accordance with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִשּׁוּם דְּקַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אַדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the method of the solution just restated.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's decision to assign the ברייתא to רבי יוסי בר יהודה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A contradiction alone is not enough reason to change who said a teaching. Doing so seems too drastic.

steps.title: רב אשי had heard the ברייתא taught in two versions
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי did not just move the ברייתא to another תנא on his own. He had heard two existing versions and chose the one that avoids the contradiction.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי heard that some people taught the ברייתא in the name of רבי יהודה, and some taught it in the name of רבי יוסי בר יהודה. Since he had a contradiction between one statement of רבי יהודה and another, he said: whoever teaches it as רבי יהודה is not precise, and whoever teaches it as רבי יוסי בר יהודה is precise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the surprise from Step 5. רב אשי was not inventing a new author. Two versions of the ברייתא already existed, and he picked the accurate one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem in Step 5 was that it sounds wrong to reassign a ברייתא just to escape a question. The answer is that the name רבי יוסי בר יהודה was already part of a known version. The contradiction only helped רב אשי decide which existing version was the reliable one.

keyTerms.meaning: there are those who teach it (this way)

steps.whatToRemember: רב אשי chose between two versions he had already received. He did not make up a new author. This closes the discussion about the contradiction in רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi heard
that there are those who teach it in the name of Rabbi Yehuda

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיכָּא דְּתָנֵי לַהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: and there are those who teach it in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda,

phrases.aramaic: וּמִדְּקַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אַדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: and since he had a difficulty of Rabbi Yehuda against Rabbi Yehuda,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: מַאן דְּתָנֵי לַהּ כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה —
phrases.english: he said: the one who teaches it in the name of Rabbi Yehuda —
is not precise,

phrases.aramaic: מַאן דְּתָנֵי לַהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר יְהוּדָה — דַּוְוקָא.
phrases.english: the one who teaches it in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda — is precise.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי שְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ דְּאִיכָּא דְּתָנֵי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the surprise in Step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual tradition: choosing between two existing versions of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב אשי reassigned the ברייתא with no basis, just to avoid a question.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two versions already existed. The contradiction showed which one was precise.

steps.title: Where do we learn that walled cities read on the fifteenth?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule about walled cities reading on the fifteenth and asks for its source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: cities surrounded by a wall since the days of יהושע בן נון read on the fifteenth, etc. From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The גמרא quotes the משנה about walled cities and asks for a source. This sets up רבא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מגילה does not say outright that walled cities read on the fifteenth. So the גמרא wants to know which פסוק teaches it.

keyTerms.meaning: יהושע בן נון, who led the conquest of ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Cities surrounded by a wall
since the days of Joshua son of Nun
read on the fifteenth, etc.
From where are these words (learned)?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that teaches walled cities read on the fifteenth.

steps.title: רבא: villagers read on the fourteenth, so walled cities read on the fifteenth
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings the פסוק saying the villagers (פרזים) celebrate on the fourteenth. From this we infer that walled cities celebrate on the fifteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the פסוק says, "Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the unwalled towns…" (make the fourteenth a day of joy). Since the unwalled towns are on the fourteenth, the walled cities must be on the fifteenth.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the source. The פסוק names only the villagers and the fourteenth, and he reads the walled cities' day from that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק goes out of its way to say "the villagers" keep the fourteenth. That implies someone else, the walled cities, does not keep the fourteenth. The other day mentioned in the מגילה is the fifteenth.
steps.confusionAlert: The פסוק never mentions the fifteenth or walled cities. רבא is making an inference from what the פסוק leaves out. That is why the next steps challenge it.

phrases.english: Rava said: as the verse says:
"Therefore the Jews of the villages,
who dwell in the unwalled towns, etc."
Since villagers are on the fourteenth —
walled cities are on the fifteenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Esther 9:19 assigns the fourteenth to villagers, so by inference the fifteenth belongs to walled cities.

steps.title: Maybe walled cities do not celebrate at all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests another reading: the villagers celebrate on the fourteenth and the walled cities do not celebrate פורים at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: villagers are on the fourteenth, and walled cities have no Purim at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's inference. The פסוק only tells us the villagers' day. Maybe walled cities simply have no day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא assumed that leaving out the walled cities means they celebrate on a different day. The challenge says it could just as well mean they do not celebrate at all.

phrases.english: But say: villagers are on the fourteenth,
walled cities — not at all, not at all!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's inference in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's inference that walled cities read on the fifteenth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק's silence about walled cities could mean they have no Purim at all, not that they have a different day.

steps.title: Walled cities are Jews too, and פורים spread through the whole kingdom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that walled cities have no פורים. They are Jews too, and the מגילה says the kingdom stretched from הודו to כוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are they not Jews? And also, it is written "from Hodu to Cush" (Purim was accepted everywhere in the kingdom).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא throws out the challenge of Step 9 with two quick reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First reason: the people of walled cities are Jews, and פורים belongs to all Jews. Second reason: פורים was accepted throughout אחשורוש's whole kingdom, "מהודו ועד כוש," and that kingdom certainly included walled cities.

keyTerms.meaning: from Hodu until Cush, the full extent of the kingdom

phrases.english: And are they not Jews?
And furthermore: "from Hodu until Cush" is written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully rejects the idea that walled cities have no Purim.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It leaves out Jews whom Purim clearly includes, both as Jews and as part of the whole kingdom.

steps.title: Maybe walled cities celebrate on both the fourteenth and the fifteenth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a new challenge: maybe walled cities keep both days, since a פסוק mentions both the fourteenth and the fifteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: villagers are on the fourteenth, and walled cities are on the fourteenth and the fifteenth, as it is written: "to keep the fourteenth day of the month of אדר and the fifteenth day of it, every year."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes a different way to read the sources. Walled cities might celebrate both days, not only the fifteenth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now everyone agrees walled cities celebrate. The open question is whether they celebrate only on the fifteenth. The פסוק "the fourteenth and the fifteenth" could mean some places keep both days. רבא's inference has not ruled that out.

phrases.english: But say: villagers are on the fourteenth,
walled cities on the fourteenth and the fifteenth,
as it is written: "That they should keep

phrases.aramaic: אֵת יוֹם אַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר לְחֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר
phrases.english: the fourteenth day of the month of Adar

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵת יוֹם חֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר [בּוֹ] בְּכׇל שָׁנָה״!
phrases.english: and the fifteenth day of it, every year"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא: פְּרָזִים בְּאַרְבֵּיסַר מוּקָּפִין בְּאַרְבֵּיסַר וּבַחֲמֵיסַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After Step 10 rules out 'no Purim at all,' this offers another alternative to רבא's inference.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's inference that walled cities read only on the fifteenth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Esther 9:21 lists both days, which could mean walled cities keep both. The villagers' verse does not exclude that.

steps.title: The extra word separates the two days
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that walled cities keep both days. The פסוק repeats the word אֵת before the fifteenth, and that splits the days between two groups.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the פסוק had said 'the fourteenth day and the fifteenth,' you would be right. But it actually says 'the fourteenth day and [אֵת] the fifteenth day.' The extra אֵת comes and separates them: these people keep the fourteenth, and those people keep the fifteenth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 11, which suggested that walled cities keep both days. It points to one small word in the פסוק that shows the two days belong to different groups.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 read the פסוק as one list: both days for the same people. The גמרא notes that the פסוק does not just say 'and the fifteenth.' It says 'and אֵת the fifteenth day,' and that repeated word acts like a divider between two separate days for two separate groups.

keyTerms.meaning: As you are saying, meaning your reading would be correct
Now that it is written, meaning 'but the actual wording is…'
A Hebrew grammar word that marks the object of a sentence. Here it is treated as a divider.

steps.confusionAlert: The proof does not come from the word 'and' (ו). Both readings have 'and.' The proof comes only from the extra word אֵת placed before the second day.

phrases.english: If it had been written
"The fourteenth day and the fifteenth"
it would be as you said
Now that it is written
"The fourteenth day
and [et] the fifteenth day"
the word "et" comes and separates:
these people on the fourteenth,
and those people on the fifteenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 11, ruling out that walled cities keep both days.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully rejects the 'both days for walled cities' reading.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That reading ignores the extra אֵת, which divides the two days.

steps.title: Maybe walled cities may choose either day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests another possibility: open towns keep the fourteenth, and walled cities may pick either the fourteenth or the fifteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say this: open towns keep the fourteenth, and walled cities may keep the fourteenth if they want, or the fifteenth if they want!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that the days are separate but raises a new challenge. Maybe walled cities are simply allowed to choose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 proved that the two days are not both required of one group. That still does not prove walled cities are bound to the fifteenth. Perhaps the fifteenth is only an extra option for them, while the fourteenth is also allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: But say, used to propose a competing reading
If they wish, meaning it is their choice

phrases.english: But say: open towns on the fourteenth,
and walled cities, if they wish, on the fourteenth,
and if they wish, on the fifteenth!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the separation of days from Step 12 and asks whether walled cities have a free choice.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that walled cities must keep the fifteenth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The separating אֵת might only give walled cities an added option, not a fixed day.

steps.title: Each group has its own fixed time
steps.stepSummary: The word בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם ('in their times') shows that each group has its own set day, so the two groups cannot share a day.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'in their times.' This means the time of one group is not the time of the other group.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'choice' idea with a word from the מגילה: בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם, 'in their times.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural 'times' tells us there are distinct times for distinct groups. If walled cities could also use the fourteenth, both groups would share one time, and that contradicts the פסוק. So walled cities are fixed to the fifteenth.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why, in practice, a resident of a walled city does not fulfill the obligation by reading on the fourteenth. Each place has its own fixed day.

phrases.english: The verse says "in their times,"
the time of this one
is not the time of that one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New פסוק brought as a source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Walled cities may choose either the fourteenth or the fifteenth.
steps.terutzMaskana: בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם shows that each group has its own separate time, so walled cities are fixed to the fifteenth.

steps.title: Maybe walled cities keep the thirteenth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if walled cities have a different day from open towns, why must it be the fifteenth? Maybe it is the thirteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say that walled cities keep the thirteenth!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that walled cities need their own day but asks why that day is the fifteenth rather than the day before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 only proved that walled cities need a day different from the fourteenth. 'Different' could just as easily mean the thirteenth, so the גמרא must still show why it is specifically the fifteenth.

phrases.english: But say on the thirteenth!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the separate-day rule of Step 14 and asks which separate day it is.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice of the fifteenth for walled cities.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A 'different time' from the fourteenth could be the thirteenth just as easily as the fifteenth.

steps.title: Walled cities follow שושן
steps.stepSummary: Walled cities follow שושן, which was itself walled and celebrated on the fifteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like שושן.
steps.whatsHappening: In one word, the גמרא answers that walled cities copy what happened in שושן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מגילה says openly that the Jews of שושן rested and celebrated on the fifteenth. Since שושן was a walled city, other walled cities follow its day rather than inventing a new one like the thirteenth.

keyTerms.meaning: Like שושן, the walled capital city where the Jews celebrated on the fifteenth

phrases.english: Like Shushan.
phrases.notes: In שושן the Jews celebrated on the fifteenth (אסתר ט:יח).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical model taken from the story itself
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Walled cities might keep the thirteenth.
steps.terutzMaskana: Walled cities keep the fifteenth, like שושן.

steps.title: What is the source for reading the מגילה on these days?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא has proven which days are for celebrating, but asks for the source that the reading of the מגילה happens on those same days.
steps.simpleTranslation: We found a source for the celebration. From where do we know the remembering, meaning the reading of the מגילה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up what has been proven so far and opens a new question. All the פסוקים until now spoke about celebrating, while the משנה is about reading the מגילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every proof so far, such as 'make the fourteenth a day of feasting,' was about עשייה, the celebration. The משנה, however, discusses reading the מגילה, which is זכירה. So the גמרא still needs to connect the reading to these days.

keyTerms.meaning: Doing, meaning the celebration and feasting of פורים
Remembering, meaning the reading of the מגילה
From where do we know it?

steps.confusionAlert: Here עֲשִׂיָּיה means the feasting and celebration, and זְכִירָה means reading the מגילה. These are two different obligations.

phrases.english: We have found a source for observing,
from where do we know remembering?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion about days of celebration and turns to the reading, which is the actual subject of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that the מגילה is read on the same days as the celebration.

steps.title: Remembering is linked to celebrating
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says 'these days are remembered and observed,' which places the reading on the same days as the celebration.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And these days are remembered and observed.' Remembering is compared to observing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק that mentions remembering and observing together, so whatever days are for celebrating are also for reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the two words appear side by side in one phrase, the גמרא learns a הקש: they share the same rules. All the day-rules proven for celebrating (fourteenth for open towns, fifteenth for walled cities) now also apply to reading the מגילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Was compared, meaning linked by a הקש
A comparison drawn from two things placed next to each other in a פסוק, so they share rules

steps.whatToRemember: Open towns (פרזים) keep the fourteenth, walled cities (מוקפין) keep the fifteenth like שושן, and each group is fixed to its own day (בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם). The reading of the מגילה follows these same days because זכירה is linked to עשייה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This links the whole derivation back to the משנה. The משנה's rule about which day to read the מגילה rests on this הקש.

phrases.english: The verse says:
"And these days are remembered and observed,"
remembering is compared to observing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק joins נִזְכָּרִים and נַעֲשִׂים, so the reading of the מגילה happens on the same days as the celebration.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The days of reading the מגילה are the same as the days of celebration: the fourteenth for open towns and the fifteenth for walled cities.

steps.title: Our משנה disagrees with רבי יהושע בן קרחה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that our משנה does not follow רבי יהושע בן קרחה. He holds that a city counts as walled for the fifteenth if it had a wall since the days of אחשורוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה does not follow this תנא. A ברייתא teaches that רבי יהושע בן קרחה says cities that have had a wall since the days of אחשורוש read on the fifteenth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings in a different opinion that argues with our משנה about which walls count. This opens a new discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה says a city counts as walled if it had a wall since the days of יהושע בן נון. רבי יהושע בן קרחה uses a much later date, the days of אחשורוש. Both agree that walled cities read on the fifteenth. They only disagree about when the wall must have existed.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two names. רבי יהושע בן קרחה is the תנא in this ברייתא. יהושע בן נון is the leader who conquered the land, and his time is the cutoff date in our משנה.

phrases.english: Our mishnah is not in accordance with this tanna.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says:
Cities that are surrounded by a wall
since the days of Achashverosh
read on the fifteenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the sources for the days of reading to a disagreement about which cities count as walled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהושע בן קרחה, a city walled since the days of אחשורוש reads on the fifteenth. Our משנה disagrees and requires a wall since the days of יהושע בן נון.

steps.title: What is רבי יהושע בן קרחה's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהושע בן קרחה uses the days of אחשורוש as the cutoff.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי יהושע בן קרחה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind רבי יהושע בן קרחה's opinion. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before comparing the two opinions, the גמרא wants to know what each one is based on. It starts with רבי יהושע בן קרחה.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה?
phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the opinion just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source or logic for using the days of אחשורוש as the cutoff.

steps.title: Every walled city is compared to שושן
steps.stepSummary: שושן had a wall in the days of אחשורוש and reads on the fifteenth. So any city walled since the days of אחשורוש also reads on the fifteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like שושן. Just as שושן had a wall since the days of אחשורוש and reads on the fifteenth, so too every city with a wall since the days of אחשורוש reads on the fifteenth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהושע בן קרחה compares all walled cities to שושן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שושן is the model city for the fifteenth, as we saw in step 16. שושן was walled at the time of the פורים story. So the test is simply whether a city was walled in that same time period.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as ... so too (a comparison formula)

phrases.english: Like Shushan.

phrases.aramaic: מָה שׁוּשָׁן מוּקֶּפֶת חוֹמָה מִימוֹת אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ
phrases.english: Just as Shushan was surrounded by a wall since the days of Achashverosh
and they read there on the fifteenth,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל שֶׁמּוּקֶּפֶת חוֹמָה מִימוֹת אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ
phrases.english: so too every city that was surrounded by a wall since the days of Achashverosh
reads on the fifteenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about רבי יהושע בן קרחה's reason.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A comparison to שושן: any city walled in the time of אחשורוש, like שושן, reads on the fifteenth.

steps.title: What is the reason of our משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why our משנה's תנא uses the days of יהושע בן נון as the cutoff.
steps.simpleTranslation: And our תנא, what is his reason?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks for the source behind our משנה's opinion. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The time of יהושע בן נון is long before the פורים story. It is not obvious why that time would matter for פורים, so the גמרא needs a source.

keyTerms.meaning: Our תנא, the author of our משנה

phrases.english: And our tanna, what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from רבי יהושע בן קרחה's reason to the reason of our משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for using the days of יהושע בן נון as the cutoff.

steps.title: A word link from 'unwalled' to the time of יהושע
steps.stepSummary: Our תנא learns a גזירה שוה from the word 'פרזי' (unwalled), which appears in מגילת אסתר and also in a פסוק in דברים about the cities in יהושע's time. Just as there walls are counted from יהושע's time, so too here.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns 'פרזי' from 'פרזי'. Here it says 'Therefore the Jews of the unwalled towns,' and there it says 'besides the unwalled towns, very many.' Just as there it means walled since the days of יהושע בן נון, so too here it means walled since the days of יהושע בן נון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that our תנא links two פסוקים through a shared word. This shows that walls are measured from the days of יהושע בן נון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in אסתר says unwalled towns read on the fourteenth. The same word appears in דברים, describing the land when יהושע came in. Because the word is shared, the meaning carries over: 'unwalled' in אסתר means unwalled in יהושע's time. That also defines which cities count as walled.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching from the same word appearing in two places
It is written here ... and it is written there
The leader who brought the Jews into ארץ ישראל

steps.confusionAlert: The פסוקים use the word for 'unwalled,' yet the result tells us about walled cities. Once you know which towns count as unwalled, you also know which count as walled.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practical הלכה that שושן פורים is kept only in cities walled since the days of יהושע בן נון, such as ירושלים.

phrases.english: He derives 'unwalled' from 'unwalled.'
It is written here: 'Therefore the Jews of the unwalled towns,'

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב הָתָם: ״לְבַד מֵעָרֵי הַפְּרָזִי הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד״.
phrases.english: and it is written there: 'Besides the unwalled towns, very many.'
Just as there it means a city surrounded by a wall
since the days of Yehoshua bin Nun,
so too here it means a city surrounded by a wall
since the days of Yehoshua bin Nun.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about our תנא's reason.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה from 'פרזי' links אסתר to דברים, which sets the cutoff at the days of יהושע בן נון.

steps.title: Why doesn't our תנא compare to שושן?
steps.stepSummary: We understand that רבי יהושע בן קרחה does not accept the גזירה שוה. But the comparison to שושן seems simple, so why does our תנא not use it?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that רבי יהושע בן קרחה does not hold like our תנא, because he does not accept the 'פרזי פרזי' link. But what is the reason our תנא does not hold like רבי יהושע בן קרחה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts why one side rejects the other's view, and then asks why the second side rejects the first. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה שוה can only be used if it was received through tradition, so it is easy to see why רבי יהושע בן קרחה might not have it. The comparison to שושן, however, seems logical and obvious. So our תנא needs a reason for not using it.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense for this one ... but for that one, what is the reason?
Because he does not hold of it

phrases.english: Granted, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
did not say like our tanna,
because he does not hold of the 'unwalled-unwalled' link.
But our tanna, what is the reason

phrases.aramaic: לָא אָמַר כְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה?
phrases.english: that he did not say like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה לָא אָמַר כְּתַנָּא דִּידַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two reasons just given and asks why our תנא does not use the simpler one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why our תנא rejects the comparison to שושן, which seems so straightforward.
steps.kashyaTarget: Our תנא's choice not to compare to שושן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The comparison to שושן needs no special tradition and seems logical. So rejecting it calls for a reason.

steps.title: Pushing back: our תנא already has his own source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised by its own question. Our תנא does not need the comparison to שושן, because he already has the גזירה שוה of 'פרזי פרזי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What kind of question is that?! He has the גזירה שוה of 'פרזי' and 'פרזי'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the question it just asked in step 24. It points out that our תנא clearly has his own source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 asked why our תנא does not learn from שושן. The answer is obvious: our תנא holds of the גזירה שוה from 'פרזי', and that sets the cutoff at יהושע's time. So the question as worded makes no sense, and it will need to be restated.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?! Said here in surprise, as if to say 'What kind of question is that?'
After all, he holds of it
Unwalled. This is the word that the גזירה שוה is built on.

phrases.english: What is the reason?!
After all, he holds of the analogy 'unwalled' / 'unwalled'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the wording of the question in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The question in step 24, which asked why our תנא does not learn from שושן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Our תנא already has a גזירה שוה that sets the cutoff at יהושע's time. So he has no need to compare to שושן.

steps.title: The real question: what kind of city is שושן for our תנא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא restates what it really meant to ask. According to our תנא, שושן reads on the fifteenth, yet it fits neither the walled category nor the unwalled category.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he meant: but שושן, whose practice follows whom? It is not like the unwalled towns, and it is not like the walled cities!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the question in step 24 really meant. The problem is how our תנא explains שושן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For our תנא, a city reads on the fifteenth only if it was walled since יהושע's time. שושן was not walled back then, yet it reads on the fifteenth. So שושן does not fit his rule: it is not like the unwalled towns, and it is not like the walled cities.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he meant. Used to restate a question more precisely.
Whose practice does it follow? Which category does it belong to?

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not asking why our תנא rejects the שושן comparison. It is asking how our תנא explains שושן's own practice of reading on the fifteenth.

phrases.english: This is what he meant:
But Shushan, whose practice does it follow?
It is not like the unwalled towns and not like the walled cities!
phrases.notes: It reads on the fifteenth, but it was not walled since יהושע's time.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: אֶלָּא שׁוּשָׁן, דְּעָבְדָא כְּמַאן?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restates the question of step 24 after step 25 rejected its original wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: Our תנא's rule that only cities walled since יהושע's time read on the fifteenth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שושן reads on the fifteenth without meeting that rule, so it falls into neither category.

steps.title: שושן is special because the miracle happened there
steps.stepSummary: רבא (and some say it without a name) answers that שושן is an exception, because the miracle happened in שושן itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said, and some say it without naming anyone: שושן is different, because the miracle was done there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about שושן for our תנא. שושן is a special exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שושן reads on the fifteenth not because of its wall, but because the Jews there rested on the fifteenth, after the miracle took place there. Other cities still follow the rule of being walled since יהושע's time. So שושן does not set the rule for other cities.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say it without naming anyone
It is different. Used to mark an exception.

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why שושן reads on the fifteenth even according to the opinion that ties walled cities to יהושע's time.

phrases.english: Rava said, and some say it unattributed:
Shushan is different —
since the miracle was done in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי שׁוּשָׁן — הוֹאִיל וְנַעֲשָׂה בָּהּ נֵס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 26.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שושן seemed to break our תנא's rule about walls.
steps.terutzMaskana: שושן reads on the fifteenth because of the miracle, not because of its wall.

steps.title: The פסוק fits our תנא well
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that according to our תנא, both doubled phrases in the פסוק teach something. 'מדינה ומדינה' separates cities walled in יהושע's time from cities walled in אחשורוש's time. 'עיר ועיר' separates שושן from other cities.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works out well for our תנא. This is what is written: 'every province and province, every city and city.' 'Province and province' is there to separate cities walled since the days of יהושע בן נון from a city walled since the days of אחשורוש. 'City and city' too is there to separate שושן from other cities.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next challenge. It first shows that the פסוק fits our תנא perfectly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each doubled word in the פסוק is read as extra, so each one teaches a distinction. For our תנא, there is a use for both doubled words. This prepares a contrast with רבי יהושע בן קרחה.

keyTerms.meaning: It works out well for... Used as a setup before a contrasting challenge.
Our תנא, the author of our משנה

phrases.english: It works out well according to our Tanna,
this is what is written:
'Every province and every city' (literally, province and province, city and city).
'Province and province' is there to distinguish

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מוּקָּפִין חוֹמָה מִימוֹת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן
phrases.english: between cities walled since the days of Joshua son of Nun
and a city walled since the days of Ahasuerus.
phrases.notes: This one reads on the fourteenth.

phrases.english: 'City and city' also
is there to distinguish between Shushan and other cities.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רבא's answer about שושן to show how the פסוק fits our תנא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For our תנא, 'מדינה ומדינה' marks the יהושע/אחשורוש divide, and 'עיר ועיר' marks שושן's exception.

steps.title: What does 'עיר ועיר' teach for רבי יהושע בן קרחה?
steps.stepSummary: According to רבי יהושע בן קרחה, 'מדינה ומדינה' separates שושן from other cities. But then 'עיר ועיר' seems to have nothing left to teach.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רבי יהושע בן קרחה: it works out well that 'province and province' separates שושן from other cities. But 'city and city', what does it come to teach?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהושע בן קרחה. One of the doubled words in the פסוק seems to have no purpose in his view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהושע בן קרחה, the only distinction is between cities like שושן (walled since אחשורוש) and other cities, and 'מדינה ומדינה' already teaches that. So the extra 'עיר ועיר' seems to be left without a lesson. The גמרא asks what it is there for.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it come to teach?

phrases.english: But according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha,
it works out well that 'province and province'
is there to distinguish between Shushan and other cities,
phrases.notes: Meaning cities like שושן (walled since אחשורוש) versus cities that were not.

phrases.english: but 'city and city', what does it come for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the בשלמא contrast begun in step 28 by turning it against רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע בן קרחה's reading of the פסוק 'מדינה ומדינה ועיר ועיר'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every doubled word must teach something. In his view, 'עיר ועיר' seems to have nothing left to teach.

steps.title: Our תנא has the same problem
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה answers by pointing out that our תנא also has a phrase that seems extra: 'מדינה ומדינה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן קרחה could say to you: Does it really work out for our תנא? He already learns from 'פרזי פרזי', so why does he need 'מדינה ומדינה'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יהושע בן קרחה by showing that our תנא faces the same kind of question. This sets up the real answer, which comes in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our תנא already learns from the גזירה שוה of 'פרזי פרזי' that walls count only from the days of יהושע בן נון. If so, 'מדינה ומדינה' is not needed to separate cities walled in יהושע's time from cities walled in אחשורוש's time. That distinction is already known. Since both sides seem to have an 'extra' phrase, the challenge against רבי יהושע בן קרחה loses its force.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you (a defense given on someone's behalf)

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not yet the full answer. It only shows that our תנא has the same 'extra phrase' problem. The actual answer comes in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לְךָ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha could say to you:
And according to the tanna of our mishna, does it work out well?
Since he holds the verbal analogy of 'unwalled' and 'unwalled',
why do I need 'every province'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה: וּלְתַנָּא דִּידַן מִי נִיחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to Step 29 by showing that the same problem exists for our תנא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-question showing the difficulty applies equally to both sides
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only רבי יהושע בן קרחה has a phrase with no job.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our תנא also has a phrase that is not needed for the basic rule, so both must read the phrase as coming for some other דרשה.

steps.title: The verse comes to teach a separate lesson
steps.stepSummary: The phrase is used for a different lesson, the rule of רבי יהושע בן לוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק comes to teach a דרשה, and it comes to teach the rule of רבי יהושע בן לוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the real answer: the extra phrase is not wasted. It teaches the rule of רבי יהושע בן לוי, which is quoted in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither side needs this phrase for its basic rule, so the phrase is free to teach a new law. That law is the rule of רבי יהושע בן לוי about places near a walled city. With this answer, the question of Step 29 is resolved.

keyTerms.meaning: It comes for an exposition (to teach a new law)
In line with the view of רבי...

phrases.english: Rather, the verse comes for an exposition,

phrases.aramaic: וְכִדְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי הוּא דַּאֲתָא.
phrases.english: and it comes to teach the view of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the defense begun in Step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the verse to a different דרשה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase seemed to have no job.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase teaches the rule of רבי יהושע בן לוי.

steps.title: Places near a walled city count as walled
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי rules that places next to a walled city, or visible with it, are treated like the walled city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: A walled city, and every place next to it, and every place seen together with it, is treated like a walled city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the rule of רבי יהושע בן לוי. Nearby places belong to the walled city's group and read the מגילה on the fifteenth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The status of a walled city is not limited to the area inside its walls. A place that is close to it, or that can be seen from it, is pulled into its status. That is why the פסוק needed an extra phrase: it widens the category.

keyTerms.meaning: A place seen together with it
Is treated as a walled city

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the halachic source for why suburbs of a walled city read on ט״ו, as in ירושלים today.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
A walled city, and everything adjacent to it,
and everything that is seen with it,
is considered like a walled city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the rule mentioned in Step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Places adjacent to a walled city, or visible from it, share its status and read on the fifteenth.

steps.title: How close counts as near?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how far 'adjacent' reaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: Up to what distance?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the exact distance that counts as 'next to' the walled city. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of רבי יהושע בן לוי says 'adjacent' but gives no measurement. The גמרא wants a clear limit.

phrases.english: Up to what distance?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the term 'adjacent' from Step 32.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The distance limit for 'adjacent to the walled city'.

steps.title: The distance is one מיל
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה (or רבי חייא בר אבא) answers that the limit is the distance from חמתן to טבריא, a מיל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said, and some say it was רבי חייא בר אבא: like the distance from חמתן to טבריא, which is a מיל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answer: places within one מיל count as adjacent. The distance is illustrated with two known towns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The limit is one מיל. The speaker gives a real-world example, the distance between חמתן and טבריא, to show how far that is.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said,
and some say it was Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba:
Like the distance from Chamtan to Tiberias, a mil.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Adjacent means within a מיל, like the distance from חמתן to טבריא.

steps.title: Why not just say a מיל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the place names were mentioned at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him just say 'a מיל'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the wording. If the answer is a מיל, why mention חמתן and טבריא?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming the towns seems unnecessary when a standard measurement exists. The גמרא assumes every detail in a statement has a purpose.

phrases.english: Let him just say a mil!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of Step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of רבי ירמיה's answer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mentioning the towns adds nothing if the answer is simply a מיל.

steps.title: Teaching how long a מיל is
steps.stepSummary: The towns are mentioned to show the real length of a מיל.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us how long the measure of a מיל is: like the distance from חמתן to טבריא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the example was given on purpose. It shows people exactly how long a מיל is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The statement teaches two things. First, the limit is a מיל. Second, it gives a familiar landmark for measuring a מיל.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us

phrases.english: This teaches us:
how much the measure of a mil is:
like from Chamtan to Tiberias.

steps.whatToRemember: Places within one מיל of a walled city, or visible from it, read the מגילה on the fifteenth like the walled city itself.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The extra wording teaches an additional detail
steps.terutzMaskana: They define the real length of a מיל.

steps.title: The prophets established the final letters
steps.stepSummary: The same אמורא teaches that the צופים instituted the final forms of the letters מנצפך.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי ירמיה said, and some say it was רבי חייא בר אבא: The prophets said מנצפך (the final letter forms).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic because the same speaker said it. He teaches that the prophets established the special end-of-word forms of מ, נ, צ, פ, כ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new subject, linked only by the name of the speaker. The claim is that the final letter shapes (ם ן ץ ף ך) came from the prophets, not from Sinai.

keyTerms.meaning: The five letters that have a final form: מ נ צ פ כ

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yirmeya said,
and some say it was Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba:
Mem, nun, tzadi, peh, kaf (final forms): the Seers said them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new statement by the same speaker as Step 34.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The final-letter forms מנצפך were instituted by the prophets.

steps.title: A prophet cannot add anything new
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this: a prophet is not allowed to introduce something new.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think so? It is written 'These are the commandments', which teaches that from now on a prophet may not introduce anything new.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי ירמיה's statement. A prophet has no authority to create new laws, so how could the prophets invent new letter forms?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'אלה המצות' teaches that the Torah was complete at Sinai. Changing how letters of the Torah are written would be adding something new. So the prophets could not have done it.

keyTerms.meaning: And can you really think so? (strong objection)

phrases.english: And can you understand it that way?
But isn't it written: 'These are the commandments',
that a prophet is not permitted
to introduce anything new from now on?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 37.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the prophets instituted מנצפך
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Prophets cannot add new things after Sinai, so new letter forms could not come from them.

steps.title: Second challenge from the לוחות begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts a second challenge from רב חסדא about the letters מ and ס on the לוחות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, didn't רב חסדא say: The מ and the ס on the Tablets...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a second challenge, using a teaching of רב חסדא about the letters on the לוחות. The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ועוד' signals an additional objection. רב חסדא's teaching about the letters on the לוחות will suggest that the final מ already existed at Sinai. That would contradict the claim that the prophets invented it.

phrases.english: And furthermore, didn't Rav Chisda say:
The mem and samekh on the Tablets

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second objection to Step 38.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the prophets instituted the final letters
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב חסדא's teaching shows that the final forms existed already on the לוחות at Sinai (completed on the next amud).
